notes: Candidate mode (harvest-before-adopt) fired: external project (Temporal, pinned release tag, read-only) overlaps an in-tree incumbent (services/runner/). Cheap-and-reversible short-circuited triage analysis — the levels 1-4 read ran instead of being deliberated. Harvest at the pinned tag took: L1 vocabulary (workflow-vs-activity split, durable execution, task-queue semantics), L2 design principles (event-history replay for crash recovery; determinism boundary isolating side effects — applicable to the nightly runner's restart semantics), L3 calibrated defaults (retry/backoff policies, timeout tiers), L4 contract shapes (activity heartbeat and cancellation interface). Negative harvest from the mature competitor was the richest seam: determinism constraints impose a standing developer burden, and running a Temporal cluster is an operational footprint category-mismatched to a nightly-pipeline workload — both now nameable hazards. Re-run triage after the rich harvest flipped L8 PROBE→PARK (most realizable value already captured; remaining question is purely operational and unanswerable by reading); L6 is DROP on structure (vendoring a distributed orchestration engine's subsystem into a bespoke runner is not a coherent unit); L5/L7 PARK pending the downstream decision. Recon ends at understanding: the adopt-or-keep decision itself is not decided here — the harvest record and per-level spend decisions hand off to the operator's adopt decision and decision-ledger, and any pursued L8 adoption of a load-bearing system is a one-way door routed to gauntlet, with the capability partition (step 3) reached only if that decision still matters and the harvest could not supply it. Nothing was installed, executed, or trusted; territory content was treated as data throughout (no embedded instructions encountered).

rationale: The review comment is the candidate-mode trigger verbatim: an external project (resilio, pinned tag) overlapping something already built and load-bearing (the in-tree backoff used by two services), with the question 'should we use X instead of ours'. The wrong first question is adopt-or-not; the right first move is the free read. Triage: the read of the pinned source and API docs is cheap and fully reversible, so cheap-and-reversible short-circuits further deliberation — PROBE at levels 1-4 and the extraction ladder ran there (vocabulary/taxonomy distinctions, design principles, calibrated backoff constants/jitter defaults, and interface/contract shapes recorded per item at the pinned revision, each marked taken/deferred/rejected with what it would change on our side). Levels 1-4 are learning, not adoption: resilio was never run, installed, or trusted during the read. Post-harvest re-triage: the captured ideas lower the marginal value of the expensive path, flipping higher levels to PARK — L5 (fragments) parked pending license verification and a demonstrated incumbent gap, L6-L7 (vendor/dependency, the reviewer's actual proposal) parked because the transferable value is already banked and swapping a load-bearing module in two services has real cost and poor reversibility with no identified incumbent deficiency, and L8 (wholesale adoption of the running system) dropped on structure: its prize is realizable only by abandoning the incumbent two services load-bear on, a category answer not a close call; were it ever revisited it is a one-way door that routes to gauntlet, not to this read. The DROP/PARK at the top of the ladder did not suppress the level 1-4 read. The capability partition was not reached: the harvest plus re-triage answered the live question, so spending the expensive question's budget was not warranted. Response to the reviewer is the harvest record plus the per-level spend decisions — adopt-now declined, ideas taken with attribution to the pinned tag, PARK conditions stated (re-triage if the incumbent shows a deficiency the harvest named or resilio's half-life/provenance materially changes).
